newsitem.title: USA: NYC may reap $750 mln surplus in FY 98 - city source.
newsitem.headline: NYC may reap $750 mln surplus in FY 98 - city source.

text.p: New York City, which expects a record surplus in fiscal 1997, might get nearly as big a windfall in the next fiscal year, if the economy and financial markets stay strong, a city finance source said Friday.

"Off the top of my head, it could come in at $750 million easily," said the city finance source, who declined to be named. He explained his initial estimate included the $200 million surplus for fiscal 1998 that Mayor Rudolph Giuliani predicted.

The Republican Mayor on Thursday proposed a $33.5 billion executive budget, which raises spending by almost $1.2 billion from last year's plan, when the two budgets are adjusted for the prepayment of debt service.
The city is using its biggest-ever surplus--$856 million--in this fiscal year to prepay debt service next year, freeing up dollars for other uses. The fiscal year ends June 30.
One financial source, eyeing increased tax revenues Albany is getting because individuals are paying higher estimated taxes than anticipated, said New York City could reap the same reward.
That could drive its surplus for fiscal 1997 even higher. "I would bet it's going to go over $1 billion," said the financial source, who declined to be named.

While noting New York City owes much to Wall Street financial houses, whose profits surged to $11.3 billion last year, Giuliani, who is campaigning to be re-elected in November, was not shy about taking his share of the credit for the city's improved finances, saying they resulted from his Administration decision to make major policy changes, like reducing taxes, a step that was criticized by fiscal monitors.

"This would not have happened if New York City had made very foolish decisions," Giuliani said Thursday. Later, he added that had he not drastically cut spending in his Administration's first few years, the city would not have seen much benefit from the extra revenues it expects to get in fiscal 1997, which are $1.3 billion above initial estimates.
"We were on our way to spending $7 billion to $8 billion more than we are currently spending, and (without the cuts) even the $1 billion tax bump would have meant nothing to us."
Fiscal monitors like state Comptroller H. Carl McCall commended Giuliani for being conservative and not relying on Wall Street to keep boosting the city's tax coffers.

New York City is only looking for this sector, whose huge profits also have helped give New York State a $1 billion to $2 billion surplus, to earn $4.9 billion in fiscal 1998. That year is expected to show a projected $200 million surplus, which also will be used to prepay debt service.

Another city source, however, was wary of rosy surplus estimates. "I can give you scenarios where our surplus next year will be greater than $200 million and where our surplus will be a deficit," he said.
The source, who also requested anonymity, added: "This budget positions the city for upside potential and minimizes the downside risk, and that's throughout the budget."

Even though Giuliani looks for a surplus next year, he based the city's budget on a forecast for tax revenues to fall one percent to $18.287 billion. That opens the door to a bigger potential windfall.
"If revenues grow by one percent, you have a two percent swing," said the city finance source, noting New York City cut estimated corporate tax revenues by 21 percent.

The city also could get another $100 million to $200 million from Washington, as Giuliani, like his predecessors, lowballed how much money New York City might get in grants, the city finance source said. He explained the extra funds typically are added when mayors modify their budgets in November.
The city's debt service estimates for next year look very high, he said, as they are based on a 7.5 percent interest rate.

"So there is a potential savings there," he said, estimating the windfall at up to $60 million. When the city in early April sold $600 million of new money, general obligation bonds, it paid a true interest cost of 6.3058 percent.

Giuliani turned up the heat on Albany, saying that while the fight might take several years, he wants a fairer and bigger share of the money the city contributes, estimating the imbalance at about $4 billion a year.
Getting more of a projected $730 million federal block grant for welfare could be a major plus for New York City, as it has about 67 percent of the state's welfare caseload.

The city finance source said that due to a mistake the state made in its federal application, Albany might get another $80 million, which if split equally with the city, would give it $40 million more.
A New York State Division of Budget spokesman was not available to comment.

Further, even though the city anticipates another 58,000 single, able-bodied adults will collect Home Relief, a joint city-state program, due to stiffer, federal welfare rules, Washington's preliminary budget pact would let legal immigrants keep getting some benefits. That could save the city, which has most of the state's legal immigrants, up to $75 million, the city source said.

While the New York City mayor wants to end in December the city's sales tax on items of clothing that cost less than $500, he admitted that it was more likely that the state--if it agreed to let the city take this step--would delay any action until April.
Every month that tax cut is delayed past December saves New York City over $23 million.
((--U.S. Municipal Desk, 212-859-1650))
